evidence_set: Quantitative PET with [11C]DASB and [11C]McN5652, 23 people abstinent from MDMA (mean 97 lifetime exposures, last use a mean of 4.74 months earlier) against 19 who had never used it. Specific distribution volume lower in the MDMA group, with [11C]DASB: occipital cortex -68%, dorsolateral prefrontal -55%, parietal -51%, temporal -48%, hippocampus -40%, thalamus -23%, midbrain -21%, caudate -14%, putamen -13%. Editors' calculation from the printed [11C]DASB means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -2.16 (-2.93 to -1.40), hippocampus -1.26 (-1.93 to -0.60), thalamus -0.62 (-1.24 to 0.00), caudate -0.40 (-1.02 to 0.21). Main effect of group p=0.01 to 0.05 by measure and tracer; 15 regional comparisons per measure without correction; the MDMA group reported more use of every other drug class listed (the illicit ones several times as often) and was about 4 years younger (Table 1; the text calls the groups well matched on age).

PET with [11C]DASB: 14 people whose use was mainly MDMA (median 635 calculated lifetime tablets, median 44 days since last use) against 21 who used neither MDMA nor hallucinogens. Binding lower by 56% in neocortex (40% orbitofrontal to 73% occipital), 32% in amygdala and 19% in pallidostriatum (group effects F=23.05, 16.58 and 7.89, p<=0.001), thalamus borderline (F=2.6, p=0.08), midbrain unchanged. The 10 people whose use was mainly hallucinogens, 9 of whom had also used MDMA (median 24 tablets), did not differ from the comparison group.

Prospective cohort scanned before first use and again about 17 months later: 59 people who had begun using ecstasy (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2, mean 18.7 weeks since last tablet) against 56 who had not (complete SPECT data for 57 users and 53 non-users). No difference in [123I]beta-CIT binding at follow-up in any region: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.031), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.035); the voxel-by-voxel analysis also found none. The groups did not differ on any imaging measure at baseline. The upper limits for frontal (0.31) and temporal grey matter (0.35) are printed as such in Table 2, checked on the rendered page, and are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035.

PET with [11C]DASB in 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions but not for at least a year (mean 2.74 years), 9 men who used other drugs and never MDMA, and 19 men who used no illicit drugs: no group effect (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, p=0.81). Regional means and standard deviations are shown only as bars in Figure 1 (p. 358); no numeric estimates or intervals are printed. Neocortical analysis was restricted to the frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio (cingulate cortex and insula were also analysed), so the occipital and temporal regions where other studies find the largest differences were not measured, and there was no group of people currently using MDMA.

evidence_set: Record of what the retracted report claimed, never evidence about MDMA (METHODS §3.2): squirrel monkeys and baboons given 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals (subcutaneously and intramuscularly), presented as modelling a regimen used at all-night dance parties. One squirrel monkey died of malignant hyperthermia and one baboon died after two doses, and in each species one further animal received only two doses, so 2 of 10 animals given the regimen died and 2 more did not complete it. The squirrel monkey that received two doses was reported at 6 weeks with caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77% and dopamine transporter -51%, against serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48% and serotonin transporter -40%. The report concluded that people taking repeated doses over several hours risk severe dopaminergic injury and possible parkinsonism, either as young adults or later in life, and argued the doses were lower than human doses (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg) after interspecies scaling.

evidence_set: PET with [11C]DASB in 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair and 50 comparison participants: binding lower throughout the cerebral cortex (46% in occipital cortex; 17% to 39% across regions after partial-volume correction) and hippocampus (21%, or 31% after partial-volume correction), unchanged in striatum, pallidum, thalamus and midbrain; the reduction held in those whose hair was negative for methamphetamine and, separately, in those negative for cocaine, and was unrelated to brain volume, cortical thickness, hormones, genotype or sex; years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001). Cognitive scores were lower on verbal memory, working memory and processing speed (effect sizes 0.43-0.86) but within the normal range, and correlated weakly with insular and hippocampal binding (rho about 0.38, uncorrected).

The one prospective imaging cohort: 59 people scanned before they had ever used ecstasy and again about 17 months later, after a mean of 6.0 tablets (median 2), against 56 who did not start (complete data sets by imaging method: 52 to 57 users and 51 to 55 non-users). No difference at follow-up in transporter binding in any region (for example thalamus -0.001, 95% CI -0.077 to 0.076) or in brain metabolites; small differences in diffusion and perfusion measures (each group's change from baseline under 5%). Before anyone had used ecstasy the groups did not differ on any imaging measure, on substance use or on transporter genotype.

PET with [11C]DASB in 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions but not for at least a year: no group effect against 9 men who used other drugs and 19 who used none (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31; region-by-group F=0.36, p=0.81), with regional means and standard deviations shown only as bars in Figure 1 and no numeric estimates or intervals, only frontal cortex among the neocortical regions measured (cingulate cortex and insula were also analysed) and no group of people currently using MDMA.

evidence_set: In 23 people who had used MDMA (of the 24 users of MDMA and/or hallucinogens), binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region except the midbrain: per doubling of tablets, -0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), -0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), -0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and -0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001). The printed upper limits for thalamus (0.022) and amygdala (0.045) contradict their p-values and appear to be missing a minus sign. Lifetime tablets were self-reported and ranged from 6 to 6590, with powder converted to tablets at 60 mg each.

Methods, 'Participants and drug use' (p. 563, the conversion of powder to tablets); Table 1 (p. 564, lifetime tablets); Methods, statistical analysis (p. 566, 23 participants for SERT binding); Results, 'SERT binding', 2nd paragraph (pp. 567-568) and Figure 3 (p. 568)

In a stepwise regression among the 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair (the degrees of freedom imply 47 people in the cortical model and 43 in the caudate model), entering demographic, drug-history, mood, subjective-effect and cognitive variables, the only predictors of lower binding across all cortical regions were years of use and maximum dose per session (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001); years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032). Lifetime tablets ranged from 4 to 922 (median 126) and maximum dose from 1 to 20 tablets (median 3), by self-report.

In 23 people abstinent from MDMA, global binding (distribution volume ratio) was related to the typical monthly dose for both radioligands (r=-0.38 and -0.37, described in the text as inverse, p=0.04 for both), on one-tailed tests chosen in advance; the authors state the study was not powered for these correlations and call them preliminary.
Methods, Statistical methods (p. 1743, one-tailed tests); Table 1 (p. 1744, sample); Results, last paragraph (p. 1745, correlations); Discussion (p. 1748, the authors' caution)

With SPECT and [123I]beta-CIT, overall binding ratio correlated with the logarithm of lifetime ecstasy tablets in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not in men (r=0.07, p=0.699). The page itself prints the coefficient as 'r=20·33', a misprint of the minus sign (a correlation cannot exceed 1), and the women's regression line in Figure 3 slopes downward. (the Lancet prints decimal points as middle dots.)

In the prospective cohort, no relation was found between the cumulative number of tablets and any follow-up imaging measure; the authors suggest this could be because of the narrow range of use, since 54% had taken one tablet or less and only 17% ten or more.

evidence_set: 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions and had stopped for a mean of 2.74 years (range 390-1825 days) did not differ in [11C]DASB binding from 9 men who used other drugs and 19 who used none (group F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31; region-by-group F=0.36, p=0.81), with regional means and standard deviations shown only as bars in Figure 1 and no numeric estimates or intervals. The authors state the result can mean either that binding never differed or that it recovered, and prefer recovery; there was no group of people currently using MDMA, and neocortical analysis was limited to the frontal cortex (cingulate cortex and insula were also analysed).

Across the 23 people who had used MDMA (the paper does not state the n for this model), scanned once, binding was higher the longer ago the last MDMA dose was taken: per doubling of days, +0.14 binding-potential units in pallidostriatum (95% CI 0.05-0.23, p=0.004), +0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21, p=0.008), +0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22, p=0.046), and no relation in neocortex (+0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67). Adjusted for lifetime tablets, pallidostriatum (p=0.02), amygdala (p=0.02) and midbrain (p=0.02) held and thalamus did not. From a log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would reach the comparison average after about 212 days, with a lower 95% limit of 91 days and an upper limit beyond a human lifespan.

evidence_set: Prospective cohort: 59 people who started using ecstasy (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2) and 56 who did not, imaged before any use and about 17 months later (complete data: SPECT 57 users and 53 non-users, spectroscopy 52 and 51). Transporter binding at follow-up, adjusted for baseline: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed; the frontal and temporal upper limits are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035, checked on the rendered page). All nine metabolite ratios were also unchanged.

Differences that did appear (each group's change from baseline under 5%), adjusted for baseline scores in Table 2; the authors report that all remained significant after further adjustment for sex, baseline verbal IQ, age, education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco, but print no estimates for that model: fractional anisotropy lower in thalamus (-8.16, 95% CI -15.30 to -1.02, x1000) and frontoparietal white matter (-8.23, -14.35 to -2.10) and higher in globus pallidus (+23.19, 3.65 to 42.73); apparent diffusion coefficient higher in thalamus (+3.68, 0.67 to 6.69); relative cerebral blood volume lower in globus pallidus (-0.083, -0.154 to -0.012) and putamen (-0.058, -0.110 to -0.006). Part of each difference comes from change in the group that did not start.
